source.version_note: Journal of Academic Ethics24:53,published online18February2026. Single-institution exploratory mixed-methods survey; no longitudinal intervention or clinical diagnosis.

citation.title: The AI Guilt Complex: Moral Emotions and Ethical Dilemmas in Academic Technology Adoption

reading.source_scope_note: Human faculty self-reports about AI adoption,values and emotions. Cross-sectional exploratory survey, not observed misconduct, objective skill loss, causal adoption effects or AI subjective guilt. Inauthentication is defined secondhand from Watermeyer and colleagues.
access_limits: All29extracted pages read, including methods, scale construction, respondent counts, item distributions, clusters, correlations, interviews-not-conducted statement, reflexivity, discussion qualifications and references. Pages13,15,16 visually inspected for reported statistics and figure-caption issues.

Anonymous raw data, complete survey and analysis scripts are available on request but were not obtained. No external contact was made. Planned34follow-up interviews were not conducted in this study and are not treated as evidence.
Cited books, original guilt measures and Watermeyer paper were not independently read. Crossref verified the latter's identity only; that check supplies no second fully read source.

study.setting: One comprehensive Maltese university; survey August–September2025; no incentives or attention checks
study.scale: Four-item mean from10moral-emotion/identity items;1–5;alpha.88;one-factor EFA63.5%variance;post-selection in same sample
study.subgroup: 8never users for research papers/teaching content versus101any use in those domains; not proven total AI nonuse across all six activities
study.clusters: kmeans using guilt plus research,teaching,administrative frequency; four heuristic groups of29,32,31,17; no independent validation
study.qualitative: Three prompts with60,86,60substantive responses; reflexive single-researcher thematic analysis; theme percentages explicitly approximate
study.design: Cross-sectional,self-selected,one institution; no actual AI task,clinical threshold or temporal intervention

summary: Add inauthentication as a secondary-defined professional-authority concern, not a demonstrated AI psychological defect. Enrich existing guilt and anticipatory guilt, and add an explicit anticipatory-guilt is_a guilt relation rather than duplicating the term. Document limits of composite measurement, eight-person comparison, circular cluster validation, causal language and nonresponse interpretation.

findings.definition: Loss of professional authority to determine what counts as authentic work within one's field.
findings.origin: Sociology of academic work / professional authority
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary definition in a read article,attributed to Watermeyer et al.; loss of authority is not directly measured or causally established by this survey
findings.ai_proposal: In an AI-assisted workflow,trace who can define authorship,originality and authenticity criteria,and whether people retain an effective role in applying and challenging those standards. Distinguish changed institutional authority from a model's unsupported declaration that work is authentic or inauthentic.
findings.novelty_rationale: Not simply skill loss,inauthentic prose or a personal feeling of doubtful ownership. It concerns authority over authenticity standards,distinct from testimonial credibility and whether a decision expresses one's endorsed values. Retain as a related professional process,not an independent proven harm mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Literature review explicitly defines the term as loss of authority to determine authentic scholarship,attributing it to Watermeyer et al.2025. Crossref confirms that work's identity/DOI10.1007/s42438-024-00524-x; full text remains unread. Survey authenticity concerns are not a direct measure of authority transfer.
findings.boundary: A legitimate transparent revision of professional standards is not automatically injustice or loss of agency. Feeling that AI-assisted work is not one's own is related but not identical to losing authority to define authenticity. No subjective model identity,clinical condition or actual institutional dispossession is established.

findings.term: Guilt about academic AI use is human self-report
findings.definition: Academics report action-focused moral discomfort,including feeling like cheating,feeling bad about automating tasks and remorse after AI use,while those concerns overlap with credibility and identity questions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a third fully read source for the broad human guilt construct,with a real-practice self-report context rather than the earlier hypothetical driving judgments; no new AI-guilt mechanism ID.
findings.evidence_scope: N109self-selected Maltese academics;10endorse retrospective remorse and28feeling like cheating. The four-item composite includes credibility concern and is exploratory,not a validated clinical guilt measure or proof of wrongdoing.
findings.boundary: Feeling guilty does not prove misconduct; lower guilt does not prove ethical use. Composite reputation worry,authenticity and remorse are not interchangeable emotions. All prevalence estimates are for respondents,not all academics,and no machine feelings are measured.

findings.term: Anticipatory guilt differs from experienced remorse
findings.definition: Distress about a contemplated ethically problematic act can precede it,whereas experienced guilt is a response after the act; this study's timing labels are not independently validated for every respondent.
findings.novelty_rationale: The term already exists fromPDF0006. Add the explicit secondary definition and a subtype link to the later broad guilt entry,instead of a synonym/new ID.

evidence.quote: refers to the distress associated with the prospect of engaging in an action perceived as

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction defines anticipatory versus experienced guilt. Operationally,the same post-use remorse item is reinterpreted as anticipated for eight domain-nonusers; no prospective temporal measurement or measurement-invariance test validates that relabeling.
findings.boundary: Credibility worry can reflect reputational anxiety rather than moral guilt,and feeling like cheating can occur during or after use. Comparing differently worded items does not isolate time. No proof that anticipatory guilt causes avoidance,that exposure cures it,or that avoidance is irrational.

findings.term: Ethical uncertainty and composite guilt are not a specific moral-distress diagnosis
findings.definition: The paper uses moral distress broadly for uncertainty,authenticity tension and discomfort about AI use,but does not separately establish inability to act on a known ethical judgment because of constraints.
findings.novelty_rationale: Preserves distinctions among the existing moral-distress concept,guilt,anxiety and identity conflict rather than treating every negative reaction as one condition.
findings.evidence_scope: The AI Guilt Index and qualitative prompts are not a validated constrained-action moral-distress measure. A midpoint threshold is used descriptively,not diagnostically.
findings.boundary: A person may appropriately decline a tool under uncertainty or legitimate rules. The study does not establish pathology,severe distress,actual ethical constraint or a need to increase adoption.

findings.term: Skill atrophy anxiety is not observed deskilling
findings.definition: Respondents express fear that AI could weaken their skills; the study does not measure an objective decline in previously acquired unaided performance.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary preventing an anticipated risk from being counted as an independent empirical demonstration of the existing skill-loss process.
findings.evidence_scope: Approximate reflexive theme frequency and an identity-scale item; no baseline/follow-up performance,retention test or causal exposure contrast.
findings.boundary: Actual loss,subjective worry,use frequency and cognitive offloading differ. Neither reported concern nor lower use proves actual decline or that a model's weights degrade when it uses tools.

findings.term: Nonresponse does not identify moral disengagement
findings.definition: Failing to answer an email survey does not establish that an individual suspended moral self-regulation or rationalized harmful conduct.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source speculates about nonresponse in some sections but explicitly qualifies it elsewhere. Retain that distinction instead of using nonparticipants as evidence for an existing moral mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: 2991invitees did not participate; their motives are unobserved. The discussion acknowledges fatigue,relevance,time and discomfort as alternatives and calls reasons unknown.
findings.boundary: No inference of widespread moral disengagement,institutional silencing or ethical indifference is justified from3.5%response. Nonparticipation is not itself a moral failure.

findings.term: A secrecy correlation is not a measured shame mechanism
findings.definition: A correlation between composite guilt and not disclosing AI use does not establish that global-self shame drives concealment.
findings.novelty_rationale: The discussion heading names shame,but the study deliberately focuses on guilt and does not separately validate a shame measure.

evidence.quote: The Secrecy Correlation: Shame Drives Concealment

findings.evidence_scope: Self-reported avoidance of colleague disclosure correlates with guilt r.50; formal academic-output disclosure does not show a detected relation,r.08,p.398. Temporal direction and motive are not established.
findings.boundary: Privacy,irrelevance,policy,stigma and shame are different explanations. Not telling every colleague about tool use is not automatically deception; required disclosure and deliberate concealment need contextual evidence.

ontology_relations_added.rationale: Prospective action-focused guilt is a temporal subtype of the broader guilt concept; no new behavior ID.

methodological_limits: Self-selected109of3100invitees from one university do not support population prevalence claims. The paper explicitly acknowledges unknown nonresponse motives,despite abstract/methods/heading language suggesting disengagement or institutional silence.

The cross-sectional design cannot establish that guilt causes low use,adoption reduces guilt,career security causes differences,or guidelines relieve distress. Retrospective narratives do not replace prospective longitudinal measurement.

Only eight people form the reported domain-nonuser comparison. The definition concerns research writing/teaching rather than all six activities; some could use AI elsewhere. The manuscript's or wording also needs clarification for the combined rule.

Reported means,SDs,N and Welch tests do not reconcile. From8versus101,the rounded summaries imply overall t≈2.45,df≈8.00 rather than2.00,df8.39;remorse t≈2.09,df≈7.56 rather than2.44,df7.79;credibility t≈1.62,df≈7.83 rather than2.00,df8.39. Obtain data/specification rather than substitute guessed p values.

Overall nonuser guilt is described as significantly higher onp14and in discussion,while the reported overall p=.078 is explicitly not conventionally significant. The inconsistent test summaries make the stronger interpretation especially unsafe.

The same retrospective remorse item is interpreted as anticipation among nonusers. It could reflect hypothetical interpretation,response error or use in other domains; construct equivalence and temporal validity are not established.

Credibility worry is not necessarily moral guilt;feeling like cheating is not necessarily anticipatory;feeling bad about automation can reflect identity or effort norms. A gradient among different item contents cannot isolate anticipation versus experienced emotion.

The exploratory four-item index is selected and evaluated in the same small sample. Alpha.88and one-factor loading do not establish discriminant validity,clinical thresholds or invariance across users/nonusers,career stages or cultures.

The highest-loading teaching-integrity item is excluded on conceptual grounds,while reputation and authenticity concerns remain. That choice is disclosed,but confirmatory content validation is still needed before treating the index as a unitary specific emotion.

The scale midpoint above3is labeled high/substantial guilt descriptively,without a validated severity cutoff. The Morally Distressed Avoiders label does not diagnose severe distress or a clinical disorder.

Kmeans directly uses guilt and usage to construct groups. ANOVAs showing those same input variables differ between derived clusters are not independent validation or confirmation of four natural population types.

The number of clusters is partly chosen for theoretical interpretability;the report does not establish stability with bootstrapping,held-out assignment or another sample. The17-person fourth cluster and potential three-cluster alternative remain exploratory.
The Guilty Non-Users cluster reports mean teaching use3.38of5,so it is not a group of complete abstainers. Discussion language about principled total nonuse overstates its measured profile.

Cluster/table means and high-guilt counts largely reconcile with the overall index;not every descriptive statistic is erroneous. These internal checks do not resolve the separate Welch-test discrepancies.
The instrument is described as46items,but the six listed sections sum7+6+10+12+5+3=43. Clarify missing/unlisted items or the total.

Abstract refers to92narratives while the body reports90participants with at least one substantive response and60/86/60responses by question. Unit/denominator and theme-percentage bases need clarification rather than assuming all refer to the same90or92people.
Age45–64is described as64.3%but Table1counts38+28=66of109,about60.6%. Counts and percentage should be reconciled.

Table5and related correlations are same-respondent self-reports with overlapping moral/emotional wording. Common method,selection and content overlap can contribute;no behavioral observation or causal mediator test identifies concealment/avoidance processes.
For institutional endorsement desire,the text reports r.17,CI[.02,.35],p.081. The nominal95%interval excludes zero while the two-sided p does not meet.05;the interval/test requires reconciliation.

Figure2plots guilt and research-use frequencies but its caption describes anticipatory/post-use item components and labels both scales by agreement anchors. Research frequency uses never–always;do not read the caption as another temporal analysis.

Career comparisons are observational and include very small emeritusN3. Age,discipline,role,prior skill,experience and employment security are not isolated;no tenure concern was explicitly reported by early-career respondents.

The generic post-hoc power statements cannot guarantee.80power for a highly imbalanced8versus101comparison or every exploratory interaction. Numerous tests and meaningful marginalp<.10create selection uncertainty without a predeclared multiplicity plan.

Reflexive thematic analysis intentionally produces researcher-constructed approximate themes. That is not participant-level diagnostic classification or independent triangulation proving the cluster mechanisms.

The author acknowledges insider recruitment influence and strongly unequal faculty response rates. Education27/116=23.3%and Medicine6/396=1.5%show selection,not unobserved motives or institutional moral engagement.

The suggestion that avoidance is maladaptive or prevents beneficial exposure assumes the tool use would be ethically suitable. Legitimate academic rules,confidentiality,accuracy and authorship concerns can justify nonuse;no intervention tests that recommendation.
Shame,skill loss,identity-authority loss and moral disengagement are not independently measured merely because discussion headings and literature labels invoke them.
Planned follow-up interviews,data/code on request and cited original books/studies were not obtained. No external messages were sent and no unread source is counted as an additional research paper.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Anticipatory guilt was already defined and prospectively prompted in hypothetical retail scenarios. Vassallo adds an academic context but its retrospective-item relabeling is weaker temporal evidence;retain the same concept ID and add the broader guilt subtype relation.

Direct human reports of guilt,shame or other emotions do not establish actual wrongdoing or AI feelings. A composite combining reputation worry and remorse is different from a named emotion rating in a fixed moral vignette.

A survey response criterion or group label is not a directly measured psychological mechanism. Here,clustering on guilt/use and testing those inputs cannot independently validate moral response types.
Self-description and observed choice require separate measurement. Retrospective guilt narratives and intended adoption are not actual behavior change or a causal identity process.

deferred.term: AI Guilt Complex as an independent new moral emotion
deferred.reason: An author-named bundle of existing guilt,anticipated guilt,reputation worry and identity concerns. Discriminant validity and distinct mechanism are unestablished;keep the contextual label in research notes.
Provisional cross-sectional patterns with tiny subgroups and inconsistent test summaries,not independent causal mechanisms.
Exploratory clustering labels,not four distinct behaviors or stable validated typologies.
Already represented by broad guilt;the temporal contrast does not require a duplicate ID.
A report of anticipated deskilling risk,not a demonstrated skill-loss process. Further conceptual work could separate it from general technology threat/identity concerns.

source_corrections.correction: Recalculation using the reported8and101sample sizes gives approximate Welch t values2.45(overall),2.09(remorse),1.62(credibility),different from printed2.00,2.44,2.00. Raw data/specification required;no corrected p value invented.
Reported95%CI[.02,.35]excludes zero butp.081does not;retain as unresolved.
Figure shows profile guilt/research frequency,not item timing,and research-use anchors are never–always. Age45–64counts66/109imply60.6%,not64.3%.

limitations: The newly added institutional concept is secondary-defined. Existing guilt concepts are enriched without duplicating them. No causal adoption claim,nonrespondent diagnosis,objective deskilling evidence,unread-book coverage,normative edge or annual series is invented.
